newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS - Boeing merger offer "not enough" - Bonn. [CORRECTED 17:00 GMT]
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Boeing merger offer "not enough" - Bonn. [CORRECTED 17:00 GMT]

text.p: German Economics Minister Guenter Rexrodt said on Wednesday that concessions offered by Boeing Co to Europe over its merger with McDonnell-Douglas did not go far enough to satisfy Bonn's concerns.
"Boeing has offered things which are not enough," Rexrodt told a news conference.
"The decisive things are the terms of exclusive contracts and the spill-over of military technology (into civilian areas) -- that is clearly not enough."
Boeing has failed to satisfy the European Union Commission the merger would not create unfair market domination against Europe's Airbus Industrie commercial aircraft consortium.

EU sources said in Brussels they did not expect Boeing to make a new offer before the Commission makes a final ruling in a week's time. Sources close to the talks said the Commission may well block the mega-merger, which would create a company with combined turnover of nearly $50 billion.

Rexrodt dismissed as insufficient Boeing's offer not to sign any new exclusive aircraft supply deals for 10 years (corrects from "...offer to limit new exclusive aircraft supply deals to 10 years..."), and to scale back existing exclusive contracts to 15 years from 25.
Boeing's offer to report regularly to the EU on any cross-subsidies from McDonnell-Douglas' military business to its own civilian operations also fell short, he added.
Germany's aerospace coordinator Norbert Lammert also said Bonn stood fully behind the Brussels commission in its tough negotiating stance against Boeing.
"A concern is being created whose turnover is as big as the whole European aerospace industry taken together," he said.
"Alone the dominating position of this...business...is hard to reconcile with fair competition and regulation."
Rexrodt's news conference was held to present a policy report which urged greater efforts to integrate Europe's fragmented aerospace industry.

He noted that the latest decision by the French government to suspend the privatisation of Thomson-CSF meant that previous plans would not be realised, but that did not rule out further international cooperation.
"The integration process in Europe, however urgently needed it is, will only take place step by step," Rexrodt said.

In comments apparently directed towards France, Rexrodt urged governments to withdraw from their interventionist role in the aerospace sector and leave the consolidation process up to the companies involved.
Governments could, however, play a "flanking" role in the allocation of subsidies and procurement contracts, he said.
Rexrodt also said both Germany and Britain were of one mind over how the Airbus consortium should be restructured into a limited liability company.

But state-owned partners Aerospatiale of France and CASA of Spain were more reluctant than Daimler-Benz Aerospace and British Aerospace to commit their assets to the Airbus company to be created by 1999, he said.
The report also said Airbus needed to expand production to survive, especially in aircraft carrying 350 passengers or more -- an area now controlled by Boeing.
It gave its backing to the development of new models, including the A340-500/600 stretch models now under review and the A3XX super-jumbo, which is in the planning stage.
-- douglas.busvine@reuters.com (Bonn 49-228-26097 150)
